Name: Miniature bronze lotus-throne Buddha (votive)
Repository: National Museum of Cambodia, Phnom Penh
Location (if different from find spot): National Museum of Cambodia, Phnom Penh
Route (if known): Bay of Bengal maritime route (Nalanda → Amaravati coast → Srivijaya → Java/mainland SE Asia)
Analytical Description (100-200 words): This small bronze Buddha, seated on a double-lotus throne, was excavated at Oc Eo, the major Funan-period port in the Mekong Delta. Its iconographic type—the elongated usnisa, the dhyana mudra, the multi-petalled lotus base—closely matches Pala-period Nalanda bronzes, suggesting either direct importation or local casting by a Nalanda-trained craftsperson. The piece exemplifies the class of portable votive objects—small enough to carry in a monk's travelling bag—through which iconographic conventions were physically transported along maritime routes. The lotus throne in particular served as a visual shorthand for Buddhist sanctity, instantly legible to devotees across linguistic and cultural boundaries. The Oc Eo find context, alongside Roman coins, Indian beads, and Chinese ceramics, confirms the port's role as a nexus of long-distance exchange in the 1st millennium CE.

Further Readings: Glover, Ian and Peter Bellwood, eds. Southeast Asia: From Prehistory to History. London: RoutledgeCurzon, 2004.

Name: Clay dharani tablet with lotus-throne Buddha
Associated people (if known): Possibly pilgrims returning from Nalanda or Bodh Gaya
Route (if known): Overland and maritime routes: Bihar → Bengal delta → Arakan coast → Pagan
Analytical Description (100-200 words): Stamped clay dharani tablets bearing a lotus-throne Buddha were produced in enormous quantities at pilgrimage centres such as Nalanda, Bodh Gaya, and Sarnath, and carried by returning pilgrims to monasteries across Asia. This example, found at Pagan, belongs to a well-documented type: the Buddha is shown in bhumisparsha mudra on a double-lotus throne, enclosed within a trefoil arch. Near-identical tablets have been found at sites in Bengal, Arakan, and lower Myanmar, tracing the overland and coastal route from Bihar to the Irrawaddy valley. The dharani inscribed on the reverse—a Sanskrit verse encoding the essence of dependent origination—was considered sufficiently powerful to sanctify a site simply by being buried within it. These tablets thus functioned as portable consecrators, physically encoding the lotus iconographic vocabulary into the fabric of new Buddhist landscapes.
References: Luce, G.H. Old Burma – Early Pagan. 3 vols. New York: Artibus Asiae, 1969–1970. | Brown, Robert. The Dvaravati Wheels of the Law and the Indianization of Southeast Asia. Leiden: Brill, 1996. | Stadtner, Donald. Sacred Sites of Burma. Bangkok: River Books, 2011.
Further Readings: Schopen, Gregory. Bones, Stones, and Buddhist Monks. Honolulu: UHP, 1997.

Name: Lotus-decorated bronze reliquary casket
Find spot: Mihintale, North Central Province, Sri Lanka
Associated people (if known): Unknown donor, possibly associated with Amaravati mission
Route (if known): Bay of Bengal route: Andhra coast → Sri Lanka → further eastward
Analytical Description (100-200 words): This small bronze reliquary casket, decorated with a continuous frieze of stylised lotus petals in silver inlay, was found at Mihintale—the sacred mountain traditionally associated with the introduction of Buddhism to Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE. The object's decoration, however, dates stylistically to the 4th–5th century CE and shows close affinities with Amaravati metalwork, suggesting ongoing material exchange between Andhra and Sri Lanka long after the initial missionary contact. Reliquary caskets of this type were eminently portable and were regularly transported as prestige gifts between monasteries, serving both a devotional function (containing relic fragments) and a diplomatic one. The lotus frieze—repeated around the entire circumference—transforms the casket's exterior into an unbroken field of symbolic purity, reinforcing the sacred status of its contents. This object illustrates how small, high-value luxury items carried the lotus iconographic vocabulary across the Bay of Bengal as efficiently as any monastic manuscript.
References: Paranavitana, Senarat. The Stupa in Ceylon. Colombo: Ceylon Government Press, 1946. | Knox, Robert. Amaravati. London: BMP, 1992. | Dehejia, Vidya. Discourse in Mirror Images. Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal, 1990.
Further Readings: Coningham, Robin. Anuradhapura: The British-Sri Lankan Excavations. 2 vols. Oxford: BAR, 1999.

column48: The vajra (Sanskrit: thunderbolt or diamond scepter) is one of the most important ritual implements of Tantric Buddhism, embodying both indestructible hardness and the instantaneous power of lightning. This bronze example, found at Nganjuk in East Java, belongs to a category of portable liturgical objects whose distribution across Monsoon Asia traces the networks of esoteric Buddhist transmission documented by Andrea Acri and others. The five-pronged form, with each set of prongs curving inward to meet at a central spherical node, corresponds to canonical Vajrayana specifications codified in Sanskrit ritual manuals circulating between Bengal, Srivijaya, and Java from the 7th century onward. Nearly identical vajras have been found at Nalanda (Bihar), at Srivijayan sites in Sumatra, and at multiple locations in Java and Bali, confirming the physical movement of standardised ritual implements along the esoteric Buddhist network. Paul Copp's work on amulets and dharanis illustrates how such objects functioned not merely as tools but as consecrated physical presences, their correct material form being essential to their ritual efficacy.

Name: Ayyavole Merchant Guild Stone Inscription
Associated people (if known): Ayyavole merchant guild members (Tamil); Lavo/Dvaravati court
Route (if known): Tamil maritime trade route: Nagapattinam → Kedah → Gulf of Thailand ports (Lavo/Lopburi)
Analytical Description (100-200 words): This Tamil stone inscription in Grantha script records the activities of the Ayyavole merchant guild (also known as the Five Hundred Lords of Ayyavole), one of the major Tamil trade corporations active across the Indian Ocean from the 9th to the 13th century CE. Discovered at Lopburi in central Thailand, it is one of the northernmost known Ayyavole inscriptions and attests to the reach of Tamil mercantile networks into the Gulf of Thailand. John Guy has documented the guild's practice of erecting inscribed stones at their commercial bases across Southeast Asia—from Kerala to Quanzhou—as both territorial markers and devotional acts, typically recording donations to local Hindu or Buddhist institutions. The Lopburi inscription, found in a region with strong Dvaravati Buddhist roots, illustrates how Tamil merchants navigated and participated in local religious landscapes while maintaining a distinctly Tamil corporate identity. Its find spot in the interior of Thailand, far from the coast, suggests that Tamil merchants had penetrated well beyond the Strait of Malacca into the continental Southeast Asian trading networks by the early 11th century.
References: Guy, John. "Tamil Merchants and the Hindu-Buddhist Diaspora in Early Southeast Asia." In Early Interactions. Singapore: ISEAS, 2011. | Abraham, Meera. Two Medieval Merchant Guilds of South India. New Delhi: Manohar, 1988. | Kulke, Hermann et al., eds. Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa. Singapore: ISEAS, 2009.
Further Readings: Andaya, Barbara Watson. "Seas, Oceans and Cosmologies in Southeast Asia." (2017).

Name: Gold Naga Amulet
Repository: Phrapatom Chedi National Museum, Nakhon Pathom, Thailand
Find spot: Nakhon Pathom (ancient Nakhon Chaisi), central Thailand
Location (if different from find spot): Phrapatom Chedi National Museum, Nakhon Pathom
Associated people (if known): Unknown owner; Dvaravati Buddhist community at Nakhon Pathom
Route (if known): Maritime and overland trade route: South India (Tamil Nadu) → Sri Lanka → Bay of Bengal → Gulf of Thailand ports → Dvaravati inland centres
Analytical Description (100-200 words): This small gold amulet in the form of a coiled naga with a raised multi-headed hood was found at Nakhon Pathom, the major Dvaravati Buddhist centre west of Bangkok. The piece belongs to a class of small personal protective amulets that circulated widely across South and Southeast Asia, their naga iconography drawing on the deep association between serpent spirits, water, and bodily protection common to both Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Paul Copp's research on Buddhist amulet culture in medieval Asia has demonstrated how such objects functioned as portable consecrators: the correct material (gold being associated with solar power and incorruptibility), correct form (the naga's protective hood), and correct consecration ritual combined to make the object an active agent of protection rather than a passive symbol. The Dvaravati Buddhist communities at Nakhon Pathom maintained close connections with Sri Lankan and South Indian Buddhist networks, and the naga amulet type found here has close parallels in Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, suggesting direct movement of both objects and their associated apotropaic traditions along the Gulf of Thailand trade routes.
References: Copp, Paul. The Body Incantatory: Spells and the Ritual Imagination in Medieval Chinese Buddhism. New York: Columbia UP, 2014. | Brown, Robert. New York: Metropolitan Museum, 2014.
Further Readings: Decaroli, Robert. "The Abode of the Naga King." Ars Orientalis 40 (2011): 142–161.

Name: Yue Ware Celadon Bowl with Lotus Decoration
Find spot: Nagapattinam harbour excavation, Tamil Nadu, India
Associated people (if known): Chinese merchants; Tamil merchant intermediaries; Srivijayan transit traders
Route (if known): South China Sea and Bay of Bengal trade route: Zhejiang (Yue kilns) → Guangzhou → Strait of Malacca (Srivijaya) → Nagapattinam, Tamil Nadu
Analytical Description (100-200 words): This Yue ware celadon bowl, produced at the famous Yue kilns in Zhejiang province and recovered from harbour excavations at Nagapattinam, is a material trace of the long-distance ceramic trade linking Tang and Song dynasty China with the Coromandel Coast of South India via the Srivijayan-controlled Strait of Malacca. The bowl's interior carries a carved lotus design beneath the characteristic grey-green glaze, demonstrating the lotus motif's pan-Asian commercial legibility: the same design that carried Buddhist significance in South Asia also functioned as a standard decorative vocabulary in Chinese export ceramics intended for Indian Ocean markets. Finds of Chinese ceramics at Nagapattinam, alongside Roman coins and Southeast Asian bronzes, confirm this port's role as a multi-directional node in the Monsoon Asia exchange network. Tom Vosmer's research on Arab shipping in the Indian Ocean and Michael Flecker's work on the 9th-century Arab shipwreck off Belitung Island (which carried tens of thousands of Tang ceramics) have illuminated the scale of Chinese ceramic export in this period, of which this Nagapattinam bowl is a small but significant South Indian representative.
